title: Gifts, Regulators, and the Companies They Regulate
hook: Two FCC officials took pricey gala tickets from Paramount while the company had billions of dollars in mergers awaiting the agency's approval. Ethics rules exist for exactly this.
key_points: Federal ethics rules generally bar officials from accepting gifts from companies with business pending before their own agency.
FCC Commissioner Olivia Trusty received Kennedy Center gala tickets worth over $12,000 from Paramount in December 2025, five months after voting to approve its $8 billion merger with Skydance.
FCC Chair Brendan Carr attended the same event in a private skybox with Paramount's CEO around the time the merger was pending.
Seven FCC commissioners have accepted Kennedy Center tickets from CBS or its parent company over the past decade, totaling more than $260,000.

Ethics experts argue that accepting such gifts should disqualify officials from later decisions affecting the gift-giver — because the appearance of influence undermines a regulator's impartiality even without proof of an explicit quid pro quo.
content_html: Regulatory agencies are supposed to referee the industries they oversee — which is exactly why federal ethics rules generally bar officials from accepting gifts from a company with business pending before their own agency. ProPublica's Corey G. Johnson reports a case that tests those rules directly.
extra_html: FCC Commissioner Olivia Trusty received Kennedy Center gala tickets worth more than $12,000 from Paramount in December 2025 — five months after she voted to approve the company's $8 billion merger with Skydance Media. FCC Chair Brendan Carr attended the same gala in a private skybox alongside Paramount's CEO around the time that merger was pending, though it's unclear who paid for his seat. Neither gift is an isolated case: ProPublica found seven FCC commissioners have accepted Kennedy Center tickets from CBS or its parent company over the past decade, totaling more than $260,000. Former Office of Government Ethics director Walter Shaub put the underlying principle bluntly: "There's no way that any top federal regulator should ever accept a gift from a regulated company with interests their work will foreseeably affect." The point isn't necessarily that a specific vote was bought — it's that accepting the gift at all creates an appearance of influence that ethics rules exist to prevent, independent of what can be proven about intent. (This card describes the U.S. Federal Communications Commission specifically.)

related.title: Regulatory Capture
related.hook: Who protects a city's drinking water when the industry that put it at risk is also the one the regulator was built to serve? That's the problem political scientists call regulatory capture.

related.title: Accountability & Oversight
related.hook: Power left unwatched drifts toward abuse. Accountability is the demand that officials answer for what they do — and oversight is the machinery that makes them.

related.hook: Corruption is the abuse of entrusted power for private gain — and it quietly drains a society, eroding trust, fairness, and the resources meant for everyone.

flashcards.prompt: What did federal ethics rules say about the gifts FCC officials took from Paramount?
flashcards.back_html: Officials generally shouldn't accept gifts from a company with business pending before their own agency — exactly the situation ProPublica describes.

flashcards.prompt: When did FCC Commissioner Olivia Trusty receive her gala tickets from Paramount, relative to the merger vote?

choices.text: Five months after she voted to approve Paramount's $8 billion merger with Skydance
Five years before Paramount had any business before the FCC
The tickets were unrelated to any FCC matter

flashcards.explanation_html: The timing — a gift arriving months after a favorable vote for the same company — is exactly what ethics rules on gifts from regulated parties are meant to prevent the appearance of.

flashcards.prompt: Why do ethics experts say accepting a gift from a regulated company is a problem even without proof of a direct deal?

choices.text: It creates an appearance of influence that undermines a regulator's impartiality on its own
It is only a problem if the gift exceeds $1 million
It is not actually restricted by any federal rule

flashcards.explanation_html: Ethics rules on gifts are designed to prevent the appearance of undue influence, not just to punish explicit bribery — the appearance alone erodes public trust in the regulator's neutrality.
